claim: MST2 undergoes autophosphorylation at multiple threonine-methionine (TM) motifs in its linker.
source: MST2 undergoes autophosphorylation at multiple threonine-methionine (TM) motifs in its linker (Figure 1A) (Ni et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ni et al., 2015 and reference to Figure 1A showing domain organization and phospho-TM sites.

claim: The pT378M motif acts as the primary docking site for MOB1.
source: One such motif, pT378M, acts as the primary docking site for MOB1.
evidence: Stated as a fact in the manuscript based on prior work.

claim: Binding of MST2 converts MOB1 to the open conformation, allowing MOB1 to bind and recruit LATS1 to MST2 for phosphorylation.
source: Binding of MST2 converts MOB1 to the open conformation, allowing MOB1 to bind and recruit LATS1 to MST2 for phosphorylation.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: Mutation of 7 TMs to AMs (7TA) in MST2 abolished MOB1 binding to MST2.
source: Surprisingly, we found that mutation of 7 TMs to AMs (7TA) in MST2 not only abolished MOB1 binding to MST2, but also dramatically increased MST2 T180 phosphorylation in human cells (Figure 1B)
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mutation of 7 TMs to AMs (7TA) in MST2 dramatically increased MST2 T180 phosphorylation in human cells.
source: Surprisingly, we found that mutation of 7 TMs to AMs (7TA) in MST2 not only abolished MOB1 binding to MST2, but also dramatically increased MST2 T180 phosphorylation in human cells (Figure 1B)
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Linker phosphorylation could inhibit MST1/2 kinase activation in a feedback mechanism.
source: Surprisingly, we found that mutation of 7 TMs to AMs (7TA) in MST2 not only abolished MOB1 binding to MST2, but also dramatically increased MST2 T180 phosphorylation in human cells (Figure 1B), suggesting that linker phosphorylation could inhibit MST1/2 kinase activation in a feedback mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that removing phosphorylation sites increases T180 phosphorylation.

claim: Truncation of the MST1/2 linker increases MST1/2 kinase activity.
source: This result is consistent with earlier findings that truncation of the MST1/2 linker increases MST1/2 kinase activity (Creasy et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Creasy et al., 1996.

claim: Autophosphorylation of the MST2 linker has dual, opposing functions in Hippo signaling: recruitment and activation of MOB1 for downstream signaling and feedback inhibition of MST2 activation.
source: Therefore, autophosphorylation of the MST2 linker has dual, opposing functions in Hippo signaling: recruitment and activation of MOB1 for downstream signaling and feedback inhibition of MST2 activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation at T325, T336, and T378 is critical for MST2 inactivation.
source: Restoration of T325, T336, and T378 individually to the 7TA mutant reduced T180 phosphorylation to various levels, indicating that phosphorylation of these three TM sites is critical for MST2 inactivation (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The MST2 3TA mutation with T325, T336, and T378 mutated to alanine was as efficient as 7TA in activating MST2.
source: The MST2 3TA mutation with these three threonine residues mutated to alanine was as efficient as 7TA in activating MST2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both T336 and T378 sites were phosphorylated in wild type MST2, but not in 3TA.
source: We showed that both T336 and T378 sites were indeed phosphorylated in wild type (WT) MST2, but not in 3TA (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by phospho-specific antibody data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Phosphorylation at T336 and T378 and the enhanced phosphorylation of T180 in 3TA were abolished in the kinase-inactive MST2 mutants (T180A and D146N) in human cells.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation at T336 and T378 and the enhanced phosphorylation of T180 in 3TA were abolished in the kinase-inactive MST2 mutants (T180A and D146N) in human cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Active MST2 kinase domain efficiently phosphorylated T180, T336, and T378 of kinase-dead MST2 D146N in vitro.
source: Active MST2 kinase domain efficiently phosphorylated T180, T336, and T378 of kinase-dead MST2 D146N in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The inhibitory phosphorylation at the MST2 linker occurs through autophosphorylation.
source: These results indicate that the inhibitory phosphorylation at the MST2 linker occurs through autophosphorylation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations showing kinase-dead mutants cannot be phosphorylated and active kinase domain can phosphorylate these sites.

claim: Deletion of the MST2 linker does not enhance either the activation or kinase activity of recombinant purified MST2 in vitro.
source: Because deletion of the MST2 linker does not enhance either the activation or kinase activity of recombinant purified MST2 in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) (Ni et al., 2013)
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and cited from Ni et al., 2013.

claim: MST1/2 interact with a specific PP2A complex called STRIPAK through the N-terminal forkhead associated (FHA) domain of the adaptor protein SLMAP.
source: A proteomic study has shown that MST1/2 interact with a specific PP2A complex called STRIPAK through the N-terminal forkhead associated (FHA) domain of the adaptor protein SLMAP (Couzens et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Couzens et al., 2013.

claim: MST2 interacted with SLMAP WT, but not SLMAP ΔFHA, in human cells.
source: Consistent with this previous report, we showed that MST2 interacted with SLMAP WT, but not SLMAP ∆FHA, in human cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SLMAP interacted with MST2 WT, but not 3TA and T180A mutants.
source: SLMAP interacted with MST2 WT, but not 3TA and T180A mutants (Figure 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SLMAP bound to MST2 mutants with a single pTM site restored at pT325, pT336, or pT378 to varying degrees in human cells.
source: Moreover, SLMAP bound to MST2 mutants with a single pTM site restored at pT325, pT336, or pT378 to varying degrees in human cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The inhibitory phosphorylation at T325, T336, and T378 in the MST2 linker is required for the SLMAP-MST2 interaction.
source: Thus, the inhibitory phosphorylation at these three sites in the MST2 linker is required for the SLMAP-MST2 interaction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental observations showing SLMAP binding depends on these phosphorylation sites.

claim: Recombinant GST-SLMAP FHA interacted with the full-length (FL) MST2, but not the MST2 kinase domain (KD) or MST2 with the linker deleted (ΔL).
source: Recombinant GST-SLMAP FHA interacted with the full-length (FL) MST2, but not the MST2 kinase domain (KD) or MST2 with the linker deleted (∆L), suggesting that SLMAP FHA binds directly to the MST2 linker in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro binding assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: SLMAP FHA binds directly to the MST2 linker in vitro.
source: Recombinant GST-SLMAP FHA interacted with the full-length (FL) MST2, but not the MST2 kinase domain (KD) or MST2 with the linker deleted (∆L), suggesting that SLMAP FHA binds directly to the MST2 linker in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SLMAP FHA requires the MST2 linker for binding.

claim: The binding affinities between SLMAP FHA and phospho-MST2 peptides containing pT325, pT336, or pT378 were 0.39 µM, 1.1 µM, and 0.16 µM, respectively.
source: As measured by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), the binding affinities between SLMAP FHA and phospho-MST2 peptides containing pT325, pT336, or pT378 were 0.39 µM, 1.1 µM, and 0.16 µM, respectively (Figure 1G and Table 1).
evidence: Measured by ITC experiments shown in Figure 1G and Table 1.

claim: MOB1 and SLMAP bind to the pT378M site with similar affinities.
source: Interestingly, MOB1 and SLMAP bind to the pT378M site (the pT378-MST2371-401 peptide) with similar affinities (Table 1), suggesting that MOB1 may contribute to MST1/2 activation through competing with SLMAP for MST1/2 binding.
evidence: Demonstrated by ITC data shown in Table 1.

claim: MOB1 may contribute to MST1/2 activation through competing with SLMAP for MST1/2 binding.
source: Interestingly, MOB1 and SLMAP bind to the pT378M site (the pT378-MST2371-401 peptide) with similar affinities (Table 1), suggesting that MOB1 may contribute to MST1/2 activation through competing with SLMAP for MST1/2 binding.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that MOB1 and SLMAP have similar binding affinities for the same site.

claim: SLMAP binding to the phospho-MST2 linker recruits STRIPAK to MST2 and promotes PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of pT180.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that SLMAP binding to the phospho-MST2 linker recruits STRIPAK to MST2 and promotes PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of pT180.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations showing SLMAP binds phospho-MST2 and is part of STRIPAK complex.

claim: Crystals of free human SLMAP FHA domain diffracted to 1.08 Å resolution.
source: We obtained crystals of free human SLMAP FHA domain that diffracted to 1.08 Å resolution and determined the structure with molecular replacement using the FHA of the centrosomal protein CEP170 as the search model (PDB ID: 4JON) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and Table 2).
evidence: Reported crystallographic data shown in Table 2.

claim: SLMAP FHA adopts a typical β sandwich fold that consists of two large β sheets.
source: Like other FHA domains, SLMAP FHA adopts a typical β sandwich fold that consists of two large β sheets.
evidence: Described from the crystal structure of SLMAP FHA.

claim: Crystals of SLMAP FHA–pMST2 diffracted to a resolution of 1.55 Å.
source: Crystals of SLMAP FHA–pMST2 diffracted to a resolution of 1.55 Å and contained two SLMAP FHA–pMST2 molecules per asymmetric unit.
evidence: Reported crystallographic data shown in Table 2.

claim: In the SLMAP FHA–pMST2 structure, the FHA domain adopts a conformation virtually identical to that of free SLMAP FHA with an RMSD of 0.33 Å for all atoms.
source: In the SLMAP FHA–pMST2 structure, the FHA domain adopts a conformation virtually identical to that of free SLMAP FHA with an RMSD of 0.33 Å for all atoms (Figure 1H), indicating that binding of pMST2 does not appreciably alter the conformation of the FHA domain.
evidence: Demonstrated by structural comparison shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Binding of pMST2 does not appreciably alter the conformation of the FHA domain.
source: In the SLMAP FHA–pMST2 structure, the FHA domain adopts a conformation virtually identical to that of free SLMAP FHA with an RMSD of 0.33 Å for all atoms (Figure 1H), indicating that binding of pMST2 does not appreciably alter the conformation of the FHA domain.
evidence: Inferred from the low RMSD between free and bound structures.

claim: Only six residues of pMST2 (D376GpTMKR381) have clear electron density in the SLMAP FHA–pMST2 structure.
source: Only six residues of pMST2 (D376GpTMKR381) have clear electron density, and bind to a surface formed by residues from the β3-β4, β4-β5, β6-β7, and β10-β11 loops of SLMAP FHA (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The pT378 residue binds at a highly positively charged pocket, with the phosphate group making favorable electrostatic interactions with side chain or main chain atoms from R32, S52, R53 and S75 of SLMAP.
source: The pT378 residue binds at a highly positively charged pocket, with the phosphate group making favorable electrostatic interactions with side chain or main chain atoms from R32, S52, R53 and S75 of SLMAP (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: SLMAP FHA prefers binding to a phospho-threonine peptide with a consensus sequence of E/D-G-pT-M-x-R/K.
source: Our structure thus suggests that SLMAP FHA prefers binding to a phospho-threonine peptide with a consensus sequence of E/D-G-pT-M-x-R/K.
evidence: Inferred from the structural interactions observed in the SLMAP FHA–pMST2 complex.

claim: The pT325-MST2320-329 and pT336-MST2331-340 peptides that do not fully conform to the consensus sequence bind to SLMAP FHA with lower affinities.
source: Consistent with this prediction, the pT325-MST2320-329 and pT336-MST2331-340 peptides that do not fully conform to this consensus bind to SLMAP FHA with lower affinities (Table 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by ITC data shown in Table 1.

claim: The mode of pT recognition is highly conserved among FHA domains.
source: Despite the differences of the loops at the pT binding site among various FHA domains, the pT-binding residues, R32, S52 and H55, can be structurally overlaid with the corresponding residues from other FHAs, suggesting that the mode of pT recognition is highly conserved among FHA domains.
evidence: Inferred from structural comparison with other FHA domains.

claim: The binding affinity between SLMAP FHA/R32A mutant and pMST2 was reduced by ~120 fold.
source: Indeed, the binding affinity between SLMAP FHA/R32A mutant and pMST2 was reduced by ~120 fold (Table 1).
evidence: Measured by ITC experiments shown in Table 1.

claim: Mutations of R32, S52, and H55 in the context of full-length SLMAP disrupted binding to MST2 in human cells.
source: Mutations of these three conserved residues in the context of full-length SLMAP disrupted binding to MST2 in human cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D), validating the importance of the pT-binding site of SLMAP in MST2 binding.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: SLMAP depletion increased pT180 of MST2 WT.
source: SLMAP depletion increased pT180 of MST2 WT (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SLMAP-binding-deficient MST2 3TA mutant had a pT180 level similar to that of MST2 WT in SLMAP RNAi cells.
source: SLMAP-binding-deficient MST2 3TA mutant had a pT180 level similar to that of MST2 WT in SLMAP RNAi cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Depletion of SLMAP did not further increase pT180 of MST2 3TA.
source: Depletion of SLMAP did not further increase pT180 of MST2 3TA.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Depletion of STRIP1 increased T180 phosphorylation of MST2.
source: Depletion of STRIP1, a core component of the STRIPAK complex (Goudreault et al., 2009), similarly increased T180 phosphorylation of MST2, and this increase was blocked by the ectopic expression of RNAi-resistant FLAG-STRIP1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: STRIPAKSLMAP is involved in suppressing MST2 activation.
source: These results suggest that STRIPAKSLMAP is involved in suppressing MST2 activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from RNAi experiments showing depletion of SLMAP or STRIP1 increases MST2 activation.

claim: SLMAP knockout cells at low densities showed increased T-loop phosphorylation of MST1/2 and elevated MOB1 phosphorylation at T35.
source: Compared to control cells, SLMAP knockout (KO) cells at low densities showed increased T-loop phosphorylation of MST1/2 and elevated MOB1 phosphorylation at T35 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Phosphorylation of LATS1/2 hydrophobic motif (HM) and YAP was increased in SLMAP KO cells without contact inhibition.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation of LATS1/2 hydrophobic motif (HM) and YAP was also increased in these cells without contact inhibition.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: A higher percentage of SLMAP KO cells exhibited cytoplasmic localization of YAP.
source: Consistent with the spontaneous activation of the Hippo pathway, a higher percentage of SLMAP KO cells exhibited cytoplasmic localization of YAP (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Expression of CTGF and CYR61 was reduced in SLMAP KO cells.
source: As determined by real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR), expression of two well-established Hippo target genes, Connective Tissue Growth Factor (CTGF) and Cysteine Rich Angiogenic Inducer 61 (CYR61) (Zhao et al., 2008a), was reduced in SLMAP KO cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Expression of SLMAP WT, but not ΔFHA, rescued the phenotypes of SLMAP KO cells.
source: Furthermore, expression of SLMAP WT, but not ∆FHA, rescued the phenotypes of SLMAP KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: STRIPAKSLMAP is a key negative regulator of Hippo signaling in human cells.
source: These results establish STRIPAKSLMAP as a key negative regulator of Hippo signaling in human cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing SLMAP deletion activates Hippo signaling.

claim: Inactivation of STRIPAKSLMAP leads to spontaneous activation of the Hippo pathway without contact inhibition or other upstream signals.
source: Inactivation of STRIPAKSLMAP leads to spontaneous activation of the Hippo pathway without contact inhibition or other upstream signals.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing SLMAP KO cells have activated Hippo pathway at low density.

claim: Addition of LatB to MCF10A cells induced MST1/2 T-loop phosphorylation and MOB1 T35 phosphorylation, as well as downstream phosphorylation of LATS1/2 and YAP.
source: We show that addition of LatB to MCF10A cells induced MST1/2 T-loop phosphorylation and MOB1 T35 phosphorylation, as well as downstream phosphorylation of LATS1/2 and YAP (Figure 3A), indicating that MST1/2 activation can turn on Hippo signaling through disruption of the actin cytoskeleton in human cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MST1/2 activation can turn on Hippo signaling through disruption of the actin cytoskeleton in human cells.
source: We show that addition of LatB to MCF10A cells induced MST1/2 T-loop phosphorylation and MOB1 T35 phosphorylation, as well as downstream phosphorylation of LATS1/2 and YAP (Figure 3A), indicating that MST1/2 activation can turn on Hippo signaling through disruption of the actin cytoskeleton in human cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LatB treatment activates the Hippo pathway.

claim: The levels of MST1/2, MOB1, LATS1/2, and YAP phosphorylation were reduced in SAV1 KO cells with or without LatB treatment.
source: In addition, the levels of all these phosphorylation events were reduced in SAV1 KO cells with or without LatB treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The relative mRNA levels of CTGF and CYR61 in SAV1 KO cells were significantly higher than those in control cells, with or without LatB treatment.
source: Consistent with the defective MST-LATS kinase activation, the relative mRNA levels of Hippo target genes, CTGF and CYR61, in SAV1 KO cells were significantly higher than those in control cells, with or without LatB treatment (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SAV1 is required for efficient MST1/2 activation during Hippo signaling in human cells.
source: These data indicate that SAV1 is required for efficient MST1/2 activation during Hippo signaling in human cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing SAV1 deletion reduces MST1/2 activation.

claim: A recombinant SAV1 fragment containing the SARAH domain did not stimulate the MST2 kinase activity toward MOB1 in vitro.
source: Unexpectedly, a recombinant SAV1 fragment containing the SARAH domain did not stimulate the MST2 kinase activity toward MOB1 in vitro (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SAV1 binding to MST2 does not directly stimulate its kinase activity.
source: Thus, SAV1 binding to MST2 does not directly stimulate its kinase activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro kinase assay showing no stimulation.

claim: SAV1 promotes MST1/2 activation in human cells likely through an indirect mechanism.
source: Instead, SAV1 promotes MST1/2 activation in human cells likely through an indirect mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SAV1 does not directly stimulate MST2 kinase activity in vitro but is required for activation in cells.

claim: MST2–SAV1 does not form an expected heterotetramer through a four-helix bundle formed by their SARAH domains.
source: Surprisingly, MST2–SAV1 does not form an expected heterotetramer through a four-helix bundle formed by their SARAH domains.
evidence: Observed in the crystal structure of MST2–SAV1.

claim: SAV1 SARAH and MST2 SARAH form a heterodimer, similar to that formed by the SARAH domains of MST2 and RASSF5.
source: Instead, SAV1 SARAH and MST2 SARAH form a heterodimer, similar to that formed by the SARAH domains of MST2 and one of the RASSF family of tumor suppressors, RASSF5 (Figure 4C and D) (Ni et al., 2013).
evidence: Observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The MST2 kinase domain in MST2–SAV1 is structurally very similar to the MST2 kinase alone, except that the T-loop helix observed in the MST2 kinase structure is not visible in the MST2–SAV1 structure.
source: The MST2 kinase domain in MST2–SAV1 is structurally very similar to the MST2 kinase alone, except that the T-loop helix observed in the MST2 kinase structure is not visible in the MST2–SAV1 structure.
evidence: Observed by comparing crystal structures.

claim: The K56-E70 salt bridge between strand β3 and helix αC is not formed in MST2–SAV1, consistent with MST2 adopting the inactive conformation.
source: The K56-E70 salt bridge between strand β3 and helix αC is not formed in MST2–SAV1, consistent with MST2 adopting the inactive conformation.
evidence: Observed in the crystal structure and interpreted based on knowledge of kinase activation.

claim: The SARAH domains of MST2 and SAV1 form a long antiparallel coiled coil and do not directly contact the kinase domain.
source: The SARAH domains of MST2 and SAV1 form a long antiparallel coiled coil and do not directly contact the kinase domain.
evidence: Observed in the crystal structure.

claim: dRASSF has been shown to restrict Hippo activity by competing with SAV for binding to Hippo.
source: The Drosophila RASSF ortholog (dRASSF) has previously been shown to restrict Hippo (The Drosophila MST1/2 ortholog) activity by competing with SAV for binding to Hippo, and dRASSF-associated Hippo is inactive whereas SAV-associated Hippo is active (Polesello et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Polesello et al., 2006.

claim: RASSF5 and RASSF1 can suppress MST1 activation both in vitro and in mammalian cells.
source: Consistently, RASSF5 and RASSF1 (the founding member of the RASSF family) can suppress MST1 activation both in vitro and in mammalian cells (Praskova et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Praskova et al., 2004.

claim: The MST2-binding interface residues are conserved between SAV1 SARAH and RASSF5 SARAH.
source: Interestingly, the MST2-binding interface residues are conserved between SAV1 SARAH and RASSF5 SARAH (Figure 4E).
evidence: Observed by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The SAV1- and RASSF5-binding surfaces of MST2 SARAH are virtually identical.
source: Furthermore, the SAV1- and RASSF5-binding surfaces of MST2 SARAH are virtually identical (Figure 4C and D), readily explaining mutually exclusive binding of SAV1 and RASSF5 to MST2.
evidence: Observed by comparing crystal structures shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: SAV1 and RASSF5 binding to MST2 is mutually exclusive.
source: Furthermore, the SAV1- and RASSF5-binding surfaces of MST2 SARAH are virtually identical (Figure 4C and D), readily explaining mutually exclusive binding of SAV1 and RASSF5 to MST2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SAV1 and RASSF5 bind to the same surface of MST2.

claim: RASSFs antagonize SAV function in Hippo/MST activation.
source: Thus, our data support the notion that RASSFs antagonize SAV function in Hippo/MST activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from structural and functional data showing RASSFs and SAV compete for MST binding.

claim: Seven interface residues (E346A, I350A, Y357A, R358A, L361A, L365A, and R368A) in SAV1 SARAH completely lost binding to MST2.
source: Among the 14 mutants, SAV1 E346A, I350A, Y357A, R358A, L361A, L365A, and R368A completely lost the binding to MST2.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro binding assay shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The MST2–SAV1 interface revealed by the crystal structure is critical for mediating the MST2–SAV1 interaction.
source: Thus, the MST2–SAV1 interface revealed by our crystal structure is critical for mediating the MST2–SAV1 interaction.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from mutagenesis experiments validating the structural interface.

claim: A SAV1 fragment containing both WW domains and the SARAH domain associated with MST2 in a complex consistent with a heterotetramer.
source: Both analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) and gel-filtration experiments confirmed that a SAV1 fragment containing both WW domains and the SARAH domain associated with MST2 in a complex consistent with a heterotetramer (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by AUC and gel filtration data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A shorter fragment of SAV1 lacking the WW domains formed a simple heterodimer with MST2.
source: A shorter fragment of SAV1 lacking the WW domains formed a simple heterodimer with MST2.
evidence: Demonstrated by AUC and gel filtration experiments.

claim: SAV1 WW domains mediate heterotetramerization of MST2–SAV1.
source: Thus, SAV1 WW domains mediate heterotetramerization of MST2–SAV1 (Figure 4H).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing WW domains are required for heterotetramer formation.

claim: WW2 of mouse SAV1 has been shown to form a homodimer in solution.
source: WW2 of mouse SAV1 has been shown to form a homodimer in solution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) (Ohnishi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohnishi et al., 2007 and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Recombinant WW2, but not WW1, of human SAV1 eluted as a dimer on the gel filtration column.
source: Indeed, recombinant WW2, but not WW1, of human SAV1 eluted as a dimer on the gel filtration column (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HA-SAV1 ΔSARAH interacted more strongly with FLAG-SAV1 WT than FLAG-SAV1 ΔWW1/2 and ΔWW2 from human cell lysates.
source: In addition, HA-SAV1 ∆SARAH interacted more strongly with FLAG-SAV1 WT than FLAG-SAV1 ∆WW1/2 and ∆WW2, from human cell lysates, confirming WW2-dependent self-association of SAV1 in vivo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The ligand-binding site of SAV1 WW2 is buried in the dimer, suggesting that LATS1/2 binding and dimer formation are competing events.
source: However, the ligand-binding site of SAV1 WW2 is buried in the dimer, suggesting that LATS1/2 binding and dimer formation are competing events.
evidence: Inferred from the structure of SAV1 WW2 dimer.

claim: Overexpression of SAV1, but not RASSF1A, enhanced MST2 T180 phosphorylation in un-stimulated cells.
source: Overexpression of SAV1, but not RASSF1A (a RASSF1 isoform), enhanced MST2 T180 phosphorylation in un-stimulated cells (Figure 5A), indicating that SARAH domain-mediated MST2 binding alone is not sufficient to activate MST2.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SARAH domain-mediated MST2 binding alone is not sufficient to activate MST2.
source: Overexpression of SAV1, but not RASSF1A (a RASSF1 isoform), enhanced MST2 T180 phosphorylation in un-stimulated cells (Figure 5A), indicating that SARAH domain-mediated MST2 binding alone is not sufficient to activate MST2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RASSF1A, which also binds MST2 via SARAH domain, does not activate MST2.

claim: SAV1 strongly elevated the pT180 signal of MST2 WT, but did not further enhance T180 phosphorylation of MST2 3TA.
source: SAV1 strongly elevated the pT180 signal of MST2 WT, but did not further enhance T180 phosphorylation of MST2 3TA, suggesting that SAV1 stimulated MST2 activation through antagonizing STRIPAKSLMAP in human cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: SAV1 stimulated MST2 activation through antagonizing STRIPAKSLMAP in human cells.
source: SAV1 strongly elevated the pT180 signal of MST2 WT, but did not further enhance T180 phosphorylation of MST2 3TA, suggesting that SAV1 stimulated MST2 activation through antagonizing STRIPAKSLMAP in human cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SAV1 does not further activate MST2 3TA, which cannot bind SLMAP.

claim: SAV1 ΔSARAH lost its ability to activate MST2.
source: SAV1 ∆SARAH lost its ability to activate MST2 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Mutations in SAV1 SARAH that disrupted its binding to MST2 (E346A/R358A and E346A/R368A) diminished SAV1 stimulation of MST2 activation.
source: Mutations in SAV1 SARAH that disrupted its binding to MST2 (E346A/R358A and E346A/R368A) also diminished SAV1 stimulation of MST2 activation.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SARAH-mediated binding of SAV1 to MST2 is required for SAV1-induced MST2 activation.
source: Thus, SARAH-mediated binding of SAV1 to MST2 is required for SAV1-induced MST2 activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing SARAH deletion or mutations that disrupt binding abolish SAV1's ability to activate MST2.

claim: Deletion of the WW domains decreased MST2 activation, with the deletion of WW2 having a larger effect.
source: Furthermore, deletion of the WW domains also decreased MST2 activation, with the deletion of WW2 having a larger effect, suggesting that WW2-mediated dimerization of SAV1 might be important for MST activation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: WW2-mediated dimerization of SAV1 might be important for MST activation.
source: Furthermore, deletion of the WW domains also decreased MST2 activation, with the deletion of WW2 having a larger effect, suggesting that WW2-mediated dimerization of SAV1 might be important for MST activation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that WW2 deletion has a larger effect on MST2 activation.

claim: SAV1 SARAH alone (SAV1 ΔN268) blocked MST2 activation in vitro.
source: Indeed, SAV1 SARAH alone (SAV1 ∆N268) blocked MST2 activation in vitro (Figure 5E).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The SAV1 ΔN198 mutant, which contains WW1/2 and SARAH domains, could support MST2 auto-activation in vitro.
source: Interestingly, the SAV1 ∆N198 mutant, which contains WW1/2 and SARAH domains, could support MST2 auto-activation in the same assay.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: SAV1 WW2 promotes the self-association of MST2–SAV1 heterodimers and enables trans-autophosphorylation and activation of the MST2 kinase domain in the context of the MST2–SAV1 heterotetramer.
source: These results suggest that SAV1 WW2 promotes the self-association of MST2–SAV1 heterodimers and enables trans-autophosphorylation and activation of the MST2 kinase domain in the context of the MST2–SAV1 heterotetramer (Figure 4H).
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing WW2 is required for heterotetramer formation and MST2 activation.

claim: The SAV1 ΔN198 mutant did not enhance T180 phosphorylation of MST2 in human cells.
source: The SAV1 ∆N198 mutant did not enhance T180 phosphorylation of MST2 in human cells (Figure 5F), indicating that the N-terminal region of SAV1 is also important for MST2 activation.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The N-terminal region of SAV1 is important for MST2 activation.
source: The SAV1 ∆N198 mutant did not enhance T180 phosphorylation of MST2 in human cells (Figure 5F), indicating that the N-terminal region of SAV1 is also important for MST2 activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that deletion of the N-terminal region abolishes SAV1's ability to activate MST2 in cells.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal 90 residues of SAV1 completely abolished MST2 pT180 signals.
source: Deletion of the N-terminal 90 residues completely abolished MST2 pT180 signals, whereas deletion of the N-terminal 30 residues greatly reduced MST2 pT180.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The FBM deletion mutant of SAV1 was deficient in MST2 activation.
source: The FBM deletion mutant of SAV1 was indeed deficient in MST2 activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of SAV1 promoted MST2 T180 phosphorylation and increased phosphorylation at T336 and T378.
source: Overexpression of SAV1 not only promoted MST2 T180 phosphorylation, but also increased phosphorylation at T336 and T378, which was required for SLMAP binding (Figure 5G).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: SAV1 overexpression did not reduce the binding of SLMAP and STRIP1 to MST2.
source: Consistent with this finding, SAV1 overexpression did not reduce the binding of SLMAP and STRIP1 to MST2 (Figure 5H).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: SAV1 prevents pT180 dephosphorylation without disrupting the interaction between MST2 and STRIPAKSLMAP.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that SAV1 prevents pT180 dephosphorylation without disrupting the interaction between MST2 and STRIPAKSLMAP.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing SAV1 activates MST2 without disrupting STRIPAK binding.

claim: All discernable domains of SAV1 are required for MST2 activation in vivo.
source: All discernable domains of SAV1 are required for MST2 activation in vivo.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing deletion of any domain reduces SAV1's ability to activate MST2.

claim: Both cytosolic and membrane fractions of MST2 were proportionally activated, as indicated by phosphorylation at T180.
source: More importantly, both cytosolic and membrane fractions of MST2 were proportionally activated, as indicated by phosphorylation at T180.
evidence: Demonstrated by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Membrane targeting cannot fully explain SAV1-dependent activation of MST2.
source: Thus, membrane targeting cannot fully explain SAV1-dependent activation of MST2.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MST2 is activated in both cytosolic and membrane fractions.

claim: SAV1 may directly antagonize STRIPAK-mediated inhibition of MST2.
source: SAV1 may directly antagonize STRIPAK-mediated inhibition of MST2.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that SAV1 activates MST2 without disrupting STRIPAK binding.

claim: The SAV1 1–198 fragment interacted with both PP2A A and C subunits in human cell lysates.
source: The SAV1 1–198 fragment, which was incapable of binding to MST2, interacted with both PP2A A and C subunits in human cell lysates (Figure 6A).
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal 90 residues from SAV1 1–198 abolished interaction with PP2A A and C subunits.
source: Consistent with the MST2 activation assay, deletion of the N-terminal 90 residues from this fragment abolished this interaction whereas deletion of the N-terminal 30 residues greatly weakened the interaction.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The SAV1 1–90 fragment bound to PP2A A subunit in human cell lysates.
source: Furthermore, the SAV1 1–90 fragment, which did not associate with MST1/2 or SLMAP (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), also bound to PP2A A subunit in human cell lysates.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The N-terminal 90 residues of SAV1 might possess certain affinity for the catalytic core of PP2A, independent of MST2 and SLMAP.
source: These results suggest that the N-terminal 90 residues of SAV1 might possess certain affinity for the catalytic core of PP2A, independent of MST2 and SLMAP.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that SAV1 1–90 binds PP2A without binding MST2 or SLMAP.

claim: Recombinant SAV1 1–90 co-fractionated with recombinant PP2A A subunit on a gel filtration column.
source: Recombinant SAV1 1–90 co-fractionated with recombinant PP2A A subunit on a gel filtration column (Figure 6C), consistent with the formation of a SAV1–PP2A complex.
evidence: Demonstrated by gel filtration data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SAV1 1–90 blocked the dephosphorylation of MST2 pT180 by PP2A A-C in vitro.
source: More importantly, SAV1 1–90 blocked the dephosphorylation of MST2 pT180 by PP2A A-C in vitro (Figure 6D).
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro phosphatase assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The N-terminal region of SAV1 can directly inhibit the phosphatase activity of PP2A.
source: Therefore, the N-terminal region of SAV1 can directly inhibit the phosphatase activity of PP2A.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro phosphatase assay showing SAV1 1–90 blocks PP2A activity.

claim: SAV1 likely inhibits the PP2A A-C core in the context of the SAV1–MST2–STRIPAKSLMAP complex.
source: Very high and non-physiological concentrations of SAV1 1–90 (100 µM) are needed for PP2A A-C inhibition, indicating that SAV1 cannot inhibit all forms of PP2A. Instead, it likely inhibits the PP2A A-C core in the context of the SAV1–MST2–STRIPAKSLMAP complex.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that high concentrations are needed for inhibition in vitro, suggesting context-dependent inhibition in vivo.

claim: When co-expressed with MST2 WT in 293FT cells, SAV1 bound to SLMAP and several core components of STRIPAK, including PP2A A-C, SIKE1, and STRIP1.
source: When co-expressed with MST2 WT in 293FT cells, SAV1 bound to SLMAP and several core components of STRIPAK, including PP2A A-C, SIKE1, and STRIP1 (Figure 7A), suggesting that MST2–SAV1 could form a complex with STRIPAKSLMAP.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MST2–SAV1 could form a complex with STRIPAKSLMAP.
source: When co-expressed with MST2 WT in 293FT cells, SAV1 bound to SLMAP and several core components of STRIPAK, including PP2A A-C, SIKE1, and STRIP1 (Figure 7A), suggesting that MST2–SAV1 could form a complex with STRIPAKSLMAP.
evidence: Inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data showing SAV1 binds STRIPAK components when co-expressed with MST2.

claim: When co-expressed with MST2 7TA, SAV1 still interacted with PP2A A-C, albeit more weakly.
source: When co-expressed with MST2 7TA, SAV1 still interacted with PP2A A-C, albeit more weakly, consistent with a direct, transient interaction between the N-terminal region of SAV1 and the PP2A A-C catalytic core.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SLMAP/SAV1 DKO cells exhibited a very similar phenotype as that of SLMAP KO cells.
source: Strikingly, SLMAP/SAV1 DKO cells exhibited a very similar phenotype as that of SLMAP KO cells.
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting and qPCR data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Deletion of SLMAP bypasses the function of SAV1 in Hippo signaling at least in un-stimulated cells.
source: Thus, deletion of SLMAP bypasses the function of SAV1 in Hippo signaling at least in un-stimulated cells.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that SLMAP/SAV1 DKO cells have a similar phenotype to SLMAP KO cells.

claim: A major function of SAV1 in the Hippo pathway is to counteract the suppression of MST activation by STRIPAKSLMAP.
source: These results strongly suggest that a major function of SAV1 in the Hippo pathway is to counteract the suppression of MST activation by STRIPAKSLMAP.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing SAV1 antagonizes STRIPAK and SLMAP deletion bypasses SAV1 requirement.

claim: The Hippo pathway is a critical signaling pathway that controls tissue growth and homeostasis.
source: The Hippo pathway is a critical signaling pathway that controls tissue growth and homeostasis.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the manuscript.

claim: MST2 undergoes constitutive trans-autophosphorylation at T180 and several residues in its linker.
source: MST2 undergoes constitutive trans-autophosphorylation at T180 and several residues in its linker.
evidence: Stated as a fact based on the study's findings.

claim: Upon activation of the Hippo pathway by contact inhibition or cytoskeletal perturbation, SAV1 binds to MST2 and forms a SAV1–MST2 heterodimer through their SARAH domains.
source: Upon activation of the Hippo pathway by contact inhibition or cytoskeletal perturbation, SAV1 binds to MST2 and forms a SAV1–MST2 heterodimer through their SARAH domains.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from structural and functional studies in the manuscript.

claim: SAV1 WW domains further dimerize to promote the formation of a SAV1-MST heterotetramer.
source: SAV1 WW domains further dimerize to promote the formation of a SAV1-MST heterotetramer.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from structural and biochemical studies in the manuscript.

claim: In the context of the MST2-SAV1 heterotetramer, the two kinase domains of MST2 can still undergo trans-autophosphorylation at T180 and activation.
source: In the context of the MST2-SAV1 heterotetramer, the two kinase domains of MST2 can still undergo trans-autophosphorylation at T180 and activation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vitro kinase assays in the manuscript.

claim: The molecular interactions among MST2, SAV1, and STRIPAKSLMAP position the N-terminal phosphatase-inhibitory domain (PID) of SAV1 for direct binding to and inhibition of the PP2A catalytic core.
source: The molecular interactions among MST2, SAV1, and STRIPAKSLMAP position the N-terminal phosphatase-inhibitory domain (PID) of SAV1 for direct binding to and inhibition of the PP2A catalytic core, thus protecting pT180 from dephosphorylation.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from structural and biochemical studies in the manuscript.

claim: SAV1 promotes MST1/2 activation through forming an MST1/2-SAV1 heterotetramer that permits MST1/2 autoactivation, and through antagonizing PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of the activation loop of MST1/2.
source: Therefore, SAV1 promotes MST1/2 activation through forming an MST1/2-SAV1 heterotetramer that permits MST1/2 autoactivation, and through antagonizing PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of the activation loop of MST1/2.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: In Drosophila, dRASSF has been reported to promote the association between dSTRIPAK and Hippo.
source: In Drosophila, dRASSF has been reported to promote the association between dSTRIPAK and Hippo, suggesting that dRASSF may also help to recruit dSTRIPAK to inactivate Hippo by dephosphorylation of its activation loop (Ribeiro et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ribeiro et al., 2010.

claim: Binding to RASSF could provide an alternative mechanism for STRIPAK recruitment to inactivate MST1/2 and block Hippo signaling.
source: Therefore, binding to RASSF could provide an alternative mechanism for STRIPAK recruitment to inactivate MST1/2 and block Hippo signaling.
evidence: Speculated based on the observation that RASSF binds MST and can recruit STRIPAK.

claim: MOB1 can compete with SLMAP for binding to overlapping sets of phospho-residues and further enhance MST1/2 activation in a feed-forward mechanism.
source: MOB1 can thus compete with SLMAP for binding to overlapping sets of phospho-residues and further enhance MST1/2 activation in a feed-forward mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that MOB1 and SLMAP bind to the same phospho-sites with similar affinities.

claim: Deletion of SLMAP bypasses the requirement of SAV1 in Hippo pathway activation in normal growth conditions.
source: Deletion of SLMAP bypasses the requirement of SAV1 in Hippo pathway activation in normal growth conditions, providing conclusive evidence for the antagonism between SAV1 and STRIPAKSLMAPin vivo.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing SLMAP/SAV1 DKO cells have a similar phenotype to SLMAP KO cells.

claim: It is unlikely that all SAV1 functions can be bypassed by SLMAP deletion, given the wide array of upstream stimuli that can activate the Hippo pathway.
source: On the other hand, it is unlikely that all SAV1 functions can be bypassed by SLMAP deletion, given the wide array of upstream stimuli that can activate the Hippo pathway.
evidence: Speculated based on the complexity of Hippo pathway regulation.
